claim: Human decisions are based on finite information, which makes them inherently imprecise.
source: Human decisions are based on finite information, which makes them inherently imprecise.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract that frames the research question.

claim: The optimal sampling process that maximizes perceptual accuracy or fitness differs when detailed information about the current contextual distribution is costly.
source: We characterize the sampling process that maximizes perceptual accuracy or fitness under the often-adopted assumption that full adaptation to an environmental distribution is possible, and show how the optimal process differs when detailed information about the current contextual distribution is costly.
evidence: This claim is supported by the theoretical derivations and comparisons presented in the Results section.

claim: Humans efficiently adapt to contextual distributions in numerosity discrimination tasks in a way predicted by models where people must economize on environmental information.
source: We tested this theory on a numerosity discrimination task, and found that humans efficiently adapt to contextual distributions, but in the way predicted by the model in which people must economize on environmental information.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiments 1, 2, and 3 showing that DbS model best fits human behavior.

claim: Understanding decision behavior requires accounting for biological restrictions on information coding.
source: Thus, understanding decision behavior requires that we account for biological restrictions on information coding, challenging the often-adopted assumption of precise prior knowledge in higher-level decision systems.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the theoretical and empirical findings of the study.

claim: Efficient coding principles have primarily been applied to early stages of sensory processing.
source: While early applications of efficient coding theory have primarily been to early stages of sensory processing (Laughlin, 1981; Ganguli and Simoncelli, 2014; Wei and Stocker, 2015), it is worth considering whether similar principles may also shape the structure of internal representations of higher-level concepts, such as the perceptions of value that underlie economic decision making (Louie and Glimcher, 2012; Polanía et al., 2019; Rustichini et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on efficient coding.

claim: Neural systems at many levels transmit information via discrete stochastic events.
source: Our restriction to representations made up of binary signals is in conformity with the observation that neural systems at many levels appear to transmit information via discrete stochastic events (Schreiber et al., 2002; Sharpee, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on neural information transmission.

claim: Perceived values of choice options are constructed by acquiring samples of evidence from memory regarding emotions evoked by presented items.
source: For example, it has been suggested that the perceived values of choice options are constructed by acquiring samples of evidence from memory regarding the emotions evoked by the presented items (Shadlen and Shohamy, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous theoretical work.

claim: Decision by sampling (DbS) theory posits an internal representation of magnitudes by tallies of outcomes of binary comparisons between current magnitude and alternative values sampled from memory.
source: The seminal decision by sampling (DbS) theory (Stewart et al., 2006) similarly posits an internal representation of magnitudes relevant to a decision problem by tallies of the outcomes of a set of binary comparisons between the current magnitude and alternative values sampled from memory.
evidence: This claim describes the DbS theory from previous literature.

claim: Imprecision in numerosity judgments has a similar structure to psychophysical phenomena in many low-level sensory domains.
source: On the one hand, a long literature has argued that imprecision in numerosity judgments has a similar structure to psychophysical phenomena in many low-level sensory domains (Nieder and Dehaene, 2009; Nieder and Miller, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on numerosity perception.

claim: Processing of numerical magnitudes is a crucial element of many higher-level cognitive processes, such as economic decision making.
source: Moreover, processing of numerical magnitudes is a crucial element of many higher-level cognitive processes, such as economic decision making; and it is arguable that many rapid or intuitive judgments about numerical quantities, even when numbers are presented symbolically, are based on an 'approximate number system' of the same kind as is used in judgments of the numerosity of visual displays (Piazza et al., 2007; Nieder and Dehaene, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on numerical cognition.

claim: Imprecision in the internal representation of numerical magnitudes may underlie imprecision and biases in economic decisions.
source: It has further been argued that imprecision in the internal representation of numerical magnitudes may underly imprecision and biases in economic decisions (Khaw et al., 2020; Woodford, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: The precision of discrimination between nearby numbers of items decreases in the case of larger numerosities, approximately following Weber's Law.
source: It is well-known that the precision of discrimination between nearby numbers of items decreases in the case of larger numerosities, in approximately the way predicted by Weber's Law, and this is often argued to support a model of imprecise coding based on a logarithmic transformation of the true number (Nieder and Dehaene, 2009; Nieder and Miller, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on numerosity perception and Weber's Law.

claim: The encoding rule that maximizes mutual information is the same rule that maximizes decision accuracy in two-alternative decision tasks when the organism has fully adapted to the statistics in a given context.
source: Under the assumption that the organism has fully adapted to the statistics in a given context, we show that the encoding rule that maximizes mutual information is the same rule that maximizes decision accuracy in two-alternative decision tasks.
evidence: This claim is supported by the theoretical derivations presented in the Results section and Appendix 2.

claim: The encoding rule for reward maximization is different from the encoding rule that maximizes accuracy.
source: The first observation based on this result is that the encoding rule for maximizing fitness is different from the encoding rule that maximizes accuracy (compare Equations 3 and 9), which leads to a slight loss of information transmission (Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparing the mathematical expressions and the data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The optimal noise distribution is independent of the number of samples n available to encode the input variable.
source: Remarkably, this result is independent of the number of samples n available to encode the input variable, and generalizes to any prior distribution f (recall that F is defined as its cumulative density function).
evidence: This claim is derived from the mathematical result for the optimal noise distribution.

claim: A system that evolved to code information using binary codes must be necessarily noisy.
source: This result reveals three important aspects of neural function and decision behavior: First, it makes explicit why a system that evolved to code information using a coding scheme of the kind assumed in our framework must be necessarily noisy.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the theoretical results on optimal noise distribution.

claim: The relationship between prior distribution and discriminability thresholds (d ∝ 1/f(v)) holds empirically across several sensory modalities.
source: Interestingly, this relationship between prior distribution and discriminability thresholds holds empirically across several sensory modalities (Appendix 4), thus once again demonstrating that the efficient coding framework that we propose here seems to incorporate the right kind of constraints to explain observed perceptual phenomena as consequences of optimal allocation of finite capacity for internal representations.
evidence: This claim is supported by empirical evidence discussed in Appendix 4.

claim: Decision by Sampling (DbS) represents a special case of the general efficient sampling framework.
source: We show that DbS represents a special case of our more general efficient sampling framework, that uses a rule that is similar to (though not exactly like) the optimal encoding rule that assumes full (or costless) adaptation to the prior statistics of the environment.
evidence: This claim is supported by theoretical analysis comparing DbS to the optimal encoding rules.

claim: DbS can achieve performance nearly as high as that of the theoretically optimal encoding rule.
source: While the predictions of DbS are not exactly the same as those of efficient coding in the case of unbounded m, under any of the different objectives that we consider, our numerical results show that it can achieve performance nearly as high as that of the theoretically optimal encoding rule; hence radically reducing the value of m does not have a large cost in terms of the accuracy of the decisions that can be made using such an internal representation (Appendix 7 and Figure 2e).
evidence: This claim is supported by numerical simulations presented in Appendix 7 and Figure 2e.

claim: In Experiment 1, participants completed approximately 2400 trials across four consecutive days.
source: In Experiment 1, healthy volunteers (n = 7) took part in a two-alternative forced choice numerosity task in which each participant completed ∼2400 trials across four consecutive days (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental design.

claim: Participants were rewarded either for accuracy (perceptual condition) or for the number of dots they selected (value condition).
source: Participants were either rewarded for their accuracy (perceptual condition, where maximizing the amount of correct responses is the optimal strategy) or the number of dots they selected (value condition, where maximizing reward is the optimal strategy).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental conditions.

claim: DbS was strongly favored in 6 out of 7 participants in the perceptual condition and 7 out of 7 in the value condition of Experiment 1.
source: Importantly, this population-level result also holds at the individual level: DbS was strongly favored in 6 out of 7 participants in the perceptual condition, and seven out of seven in the value condition (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by individual-level analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Performance was stable across the four consecutive days in Experiment 1.
source: These results are not likely to be affected by changes in performance over time, as performance was stable across the four consecutive days (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the performance data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: DbS made more accurate predictions than the logarithmic model of numerosity discrimination.
source: We also investigated whether the DbS model makes more accurate predictions than the widely used logarithmic model of numerosity discrimination tasks (Dehaene, 2003). We found that DbS still made better out-of-sample predictions than the log-model (Figure 4b, Figure 5f,g).
evidence: This claim is supported by model comparison results shown in Figure 4b and Figure 5f,g.

claim: Reaction times did not differ between perceptual and value experimental conditions.
source: We found that reaction times did not differ between experimental conditions for any of the different performance assessments considered here (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by reaction time data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: All sampling models and the logarithmic model have the same degrees of freedom.
source: Here it is important to emphasize that all sampling models and the logarithmic model of numerosity have the same degrees of freedom (performance is determined by n in the sampling models and Weber's fraction σ in the log model, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a statement about the model specifications.

claim: The recovered value of the shape parameter α closely followed the value of the empirical prior with a slight underestimation.
source: Then we fitted this model to the empirical data and found that the recovered value of the shape parameter α closely followed the value of the empirical prior with a slight underestimation (Figure 5a).
evidence: This claim is supported by the parameter recovery results shown in Figure 5a.

claim: In Experiment 3, the shape parameter of the prior was set to α=1, lower than in Experiments 1-2.
source: Next, we investigated the dynamics of prior adaptation. To this end, we ran a new experiment (Experiment 3, n = 7 new participants) in which we set the shape parameter of the prior to a lower value compared to Experiments 1–2 (Figure 5b, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental design for Experiment 3, with reference to Figure 5b.

claim: For Experiments 1-2, the value of α quickly reached an asymptotic value close to the target value.
source: First, we found that for Experiments 1–2, the value of α quickly reached an asymptotic value close to the target value (Figure 5c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the adaptation dynamics shown in Figure 5c.

claim: For Experiment 3, the value of α continued to decrease during the experimental session, slowly approaching its target value.
source: On the other hand, for Experiment 3 the value of α continued to decrease during the experimental session, but slowly approaching its target value.
evidence: This claim is supported by the adaptation dynamics for Experiment 3.

claim: The DbS model provides more accurate qualitative and quantitative out-of-sample predictions than the log model in Experiment 3.
source: Furthermore, we found that the DbS model again provides more accurate qualitative and quantitative out-of-sample predictions than the log model (Figure 5e,f).
evidence: This claim is supported by model comparison results for Experiment 3 shown in Figure 5e,f.

claim: The brain is a metabolically expensive inference machine.
source: The brain is a metabolically expensive inference machine (Hawkes et al., 1998; Navarrete et al., 2011; Stone, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on brain metabolism.

claim: Evolutionary pressure has driven the brain to make productive use of its limited resources by exploiting statistical regularities.
source: Therefore, it has been suggested that evolutionary pressure has driven it to make productive use of its limited resources by exploiting statistical regularities (Attneave, 1954; Barlow, 1961; Laughlin, 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational work on efficient coding theory.

claim: Noise is not the main cause of behavioral performance degradation, but rather a necessary feature of systems encoding information based on binary codes.
source: Another key implication of our results is that we provide an alternative explanation to the usual conception of noise as the main cause of behavioral performance degradation, where noise is usually artificially added to models of decision behavior to generate the desired variability (Ratcliff and Rouder, 1998; Wang, 2002). On the contrary, our work makes it formally explicit why a system that evolved to encode information based on binary codes must be necessarily noisy, also revealing how the system could take advantage of its unavoidable noisy properties (Faisal et al., 2008) to optimize decision behavior (Tsetsos et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the theoretical results on optimal noise distribution.

claim: Stochastic discrete events serve to optimize information transmission in neural population coding.
source: Interestingly, it has been shown in recent work that stochastic discrete events also serve to optimize information transmission in neural population coding (Ashida and Kubo, 2010; Nikitin et al., 2009; Schmerl and McDonnell, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on neural coding.

claim: A large proportion of LIP neurons likely reflect binary (discrete) coding states to guide decision behavior.
source: Interestingly, our results could provide an alternative explanation of the recent controversial finding that dynamics of a large proportion of LIP neurons likely reflect binary (discrete) coding states to guide decision behavior (Latimer et al., 2015; Zoltowski et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent neurophysiological findings.

claim: DbS automatically adjusts the encoding in response to changes in the frequency distribution from which exemplars are drawn in approximately the right way.
source: Crucially, DbS automatically adjusts the encoding in response to changes in the frequency distribution from which exemplars are drawn in approximately the right way, while providing a simple answer to the question of how such adaptation of the encoding rule to a changing frequency distribution occurs, at a relatively low cost.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the theoretical analysis of DbS.

claim: Relying on samples from memory might be less metabolically costly than optimal adaptation requiring complex neuroplastic changes.
source: Thus, a possible explanation of why DbS is the favored model in our numerosity task is that accuracy and reward maximization requires optimal adaptation of the noise distribution based on our imposed prior, requiring complex neuroplastic changes to be implemented, which are in turn metabolically costly (Buchanan et al., 2013). Relying on samples from memory might be less metabolically costly as these systems are plastic in short time scales, and therefore a relatively simpler heuristic to implement allowing more efficient adaptation.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for why DbS is favored, supported by citation to work on metabolic costs.

claim: In a reward learning task, a model that estimates values based on memory samples from recent past experiences can explain the data better than canonical incremental learning models.
source: Interestingly, it was recently shown that in a reward learning task, a model that estimates values based on memory samples from recent past experiences can explain the data better than canonical incremental learning models (Bornstein et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research on reward learning.

claim: Sampling from memory is an efficient mechanism for guiding choice behavior, allowing quick learning and generalization of environmental contexts based on recent experience.
source: Based on their and our findings, we conclude that sampling from memory is an efficient mechanism for guiding choice behavior, as it allows quick learning and generalization of environmental contexts based on recent experience without significantly sacrificing behavioral performance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current study's findings and previous research.

claim: Each participant in Experiment 1 carried out the numerosity discrimination task for four consecutive days for approximately one hour per day.
source: Participants (n = 7) carried out a numerosity discrimination task for four consecutive days for approximately one hour per day.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Each daily session in Experiment 1 consisted of a training run followed by 8 runs of 75 trials each.
source: Each daily session consisted of a training run followed by 8 runs of 75 trials each.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Two clouds of dots were presented on the screen for 200 ms in the numerosity discrimination task.
source: After a fixation period (1–1.5 s jittered), two clouds of dots (left and right) were presented on the screen for 200 ms.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental procedure.

claim: In the value condition of Experiment 1, participants were informed that each dot corresponded to 1 Swiss Franc (CHF).
source: In the value condition, participants were explicitly informed that each dot in a cloud of dots corresponded to 1 Swiss Franc (CHF).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental procedure.

claim: In the accuracy condition of Experiment 1, participants could receive a fixed reward of 15 Swiss Francs (CHF) for each correct trial.
source: In the accuracy condition, participants were explicitly informed that they could receive a fixed reward (15 Swiss Francs (CHF)) for each correct trial.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Each condition in Experiment 1 lasted for two consecutive days with the starting condition randomized across participants.
source: Each condition lasted for two consecutive days with the starting condition randomized across participants.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental design.

claim: In Experiment 2, each of four daily sessions consisted of 16 runs of 40 trials each.
source: Participants (n = 6) carried out a numerosity discrimination task in which each of four daily sessions consisted of 16 runs of 40 trials each, thus each participant completed ∼2560 trials.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental procedure for Experiment 2.

claim: In the perceptual condition of Experiment 2, participants had to accumulate points and reach a threshold corresponding to 85% of correct trials in a given run.
source: In the perceptual condition, a fixed amount of points was awarded if the participants chose the cloud with more dots. In this condition, participants were instructed to accumulate a number of points and reach a threshold given a limited number of trials. Based on the results obtained in Experiment 1, the threshold corresponded to 85% of correct trials in a given run, however the participants were unaware of this.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental procedure for Experiment 2.

claim: Experiment 3 was carried out over three consecutive days.
source: The design of Experiment 3 was similar to the value condition of Experiment 2 (n = 7 participants) and was carried out over three consecutive days.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental design for Experiment 3.

claim: For Experiments 1 and 2, the shape parameter of the prior distribution was set to α=2.
source: For Experiments 1 and 2 the shape parameter was set to α=2, and for Experiment 3 was set to α=1.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental design parameters.

claim: Eyetracking was used to check participants' fixation during stimulus presentation.
source: Eyetracking (EyeLink 1000 Plus) was used to check the participants' fixation during stimulus presentation.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental apparatus and procedure.

claim: Only 212 out of 45,600 trials were canceled due to participants blinking or moving their gaze away from fixation (<0.5% of trials).
source: When participants blinked or moved their gaze (more than 2° of visual angle) away from the fixation cross during the stimulus presentation, the trial was canceled (only 212 out of 45,600 trials were canceled, that is, <0.5% of the trials).
evidence: This is a direct report of data quality from the experiments.

claim: The diameter of the dots varied between 0.42° and 1.45° of visual angle.
source: The diameter of the dots varied between 0.42° and 1.45° of visual angle.
evidence: This is a direct description of the stimulus properties.

claim: Either the average dot size or the total area covered by the dots was maintained constant in both clouds for each trial.
source: Following previous numerosity experiments (van den Berg et al., 2017; Izard and Dehaene, 2008), either the average dot size or the total area covered by the dots was maintained constant in both clouds for each trial.
evidence: This is a direct description of the stimulus control procedure, with citations to previous work.

claim: The choice structure is the same for all three sampling models, differing only in their encoding rule.
source: Thus, the choice structure is the same for all models, only differing in their encoding rule.
evidence: This is a statement about the model specifications.

claim: Model fits were performed starting after a fourth of the daily trials to allow for prior adaptation.
source: In order to allow for prior adaptation, the model fits presented in Figure 3 and Figure 4 were fit starting after a fourth of the daily trials (corresponding to 150 trials for Experiment 1 and 160 trials for Experiment 2) to allow for prior adaptation and fixing the shape parameter to its true generative value α=2.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis procedure.

claim: The shape parameter value that minimizes the difference between DbS and logarithmic discriminability is α=2.58.
source: We found that the shape parameter value that minimizes Equation 20 is α=2.58.
evidence: This is a result from the mathematical analysis of discriminability.

claim: Posterior inference of the parameters in all hierarchical models was performed via the Gibbs sampler using MCMC implemented in JAGS.
source: Posterior inference of the parameters in all the hierarchical models described above was performed via the Gibbs sampler using the Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) technique implemented in JAGS.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical analysis method.

claim: A total of 50,000 samples were drawn from an initial burn-in step and subsequently 50,000 new samples were drawn for each of three chains.
source: For each model, a total of 50,000 samples were drawn from an initial burn-in step and subsequently a total of new 50,000 samples were drawn for each of three chains (samples for each chain were generated based on a different random number generator engine, and each with a different seed).
evidence: This is a description of the MCMC sampling procedure.

claim: All latent variables in the Bayesian models had R^<1.05, suggesting that all three chains converged to a target posterior distribution.
source: We conducted Gelman–Rubin tests for each parameter to confirm convergence of the chains. All latent variables in our Bayesian models had R^<1.05, which suggests that all three chains converged to a target posterior distribution.
evidence: This is a report of convergence diagnostics for the MCMC analysis.

claim: Model comparison was performed using leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO) that uses samples from the full posterior.
source: Therefore, in order to perform model comparison, we used a method for approximating leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO) that uses samples from the full posterior (Vehtari et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a description of the model comparison method, with citation.
